q: Which signal best suggests that a problem is worth building a company around?
options: Nobody has ever tried to solve it, so the field is wide open
People already spend money or hours on clumsy workarounds
Friends and family say they love it whenever you describe it
It uses a new technology that investors are excited about
why: Workarounds show the pain is real enough that people already act on it. A total absence of attempts often means few people care, and compliments or trendy technology don't show demand.

q: Which one-line description would a stranger understand in a single read?
options: An AI-native platform transforming the pharmacy supply chain
Next-generation inventory intelligence for modern healthcare
We help small pharmacies stop throwing away expired medicine
A seamless, end-to-end ecosystem for health businesses of every size
why: It names the customer and the problem in everyday words. The others sound impressive, but a reader couldn't say who they're for or what they do.

q: A founder writes: "Why now: AI keeps getting better every year." What's the main weakness?
options: It names no specific change that matters to this customer
It's too specific about the technology, so it will date
Why-now sections should cover market size, not technology
It should be cut, since readers rarely care about timing
why: A strong why-now names a specific change in technology, cost, rules or behavior and links it to this customer's problem. A trend that applies to every company explains nothing.

q: What is the main advantage of a one-page memo over a slide deck?
options: A memo can hold far more detail, such as the full product roadmap
A memo is meant for investors, while a deck is meant for customers
A memo means you never have to present your idea in person
A memo must make sense without you, so gaps in thinking show
why: Slides are usually made to go with a talk and can skip the reasoning. A memo is forwarded and read without you, so every step of the argument has to be on the page.

q: A memo says: "The global food market is worth trillions. If we win just 1%, that's a huge business." What's the problem?
options: The share is too small; a memo should claim a much bigger slice
It ignores how many customers you can reach and what each pays
Market size should be left out of a memo entirely
It just needs a source, such as a published industry report
why: A top-down share of a huge market says nothing about your plan, even with a source attached. A bottom-up estimate, the customers you can realistically reach multiplied by what each pays in a year, shows you understand the business.
